Copper August 2011 
• 
Just as the talk was returning copper back to the $10,000/t level, economic uncertainty in the shape of renewed 
sovereign debt fears in Europe, in addition to concerns over the US debt ceiling, sent copper crashing at the start of 
August.  Cash quotes declined by over $1,200/t from the end of July to the low for the month on 10th August before 
directionless trade ensued for the remainder of the month as prices bounced between $8,700/t and $9,000/t. 
• 
Prices will continue to be driven by economic news and related sentiment in the short term, while the direction of 
physical premia will likely be the first indicator of whether there has been any real impact to demand from the knock 
to confidence that the latest round of debt problems has caused.  While we still expect prices to increase in the final 
quarter, we have lowered our forecast to $9,700/t from $10,000/t previously as a result of the lower starting point that 
the latest bout of debt panic has caused.   
• 
We have made a number of changes to our demand forecasts since last month, with the net result that we now 
forecast global demand growth of 5.1% this year.  Although this change is in itself relatively modest, there have been 
more significant changes within this global number.  Of particular note, we have upgraded our estimate of Chinese 
demand to 9.2% from 5% previously, while we have downgraded both Western European and US demand prospects 
for this year, to 0.3% and 3% respectively.   
• 
Spot TC/RC sales to traders declined below $50/t & 5c/lb during August as strikes and stock drawdowns weighed.  
There are several factors supporting these lower numbers, including the effects of the force majeure declared by 
Escondida during recent industrial action at the mine that forced various smelters in Asia to cover the resultant 
shortfall, either from the spot market or through other suppliers advancing tonnage.  The other factor relates to the 
ongoing decline in what had been a large inventory of concentrates in China, which contributed to lower spot rates 
and has eroded the CSPT’s desired floor price for purchases by a further $10/t & 1c/lb to $90/t & 9c/lb this month.

Copper Monthly Update 
Market Developments 
Sell in May and then again in August  Just as the talk was returning copper back to the $10,000/t level, economic 
uncertainty in the shape of renewed sovereign debt fears in Europe, in addition to concerns over the US debt ceiling sent 
copper crashing at the start of August.  Cash quotes declined by over $1,200/t from the end of July to the low for the 
month on 10th August before directionless trade ensued for the remainder of the month as prices bounced between 
$8,700/t and $9,000/t. 
Debt deals didn’t dampen demand doubt driven declines  The price declines in the first few days of the month were 
relatively gentle, despite concerns over the potential for a US debt default as US lawmakers wrangled over raising their 
debt ceiling.  That Democrats and Republicans managed to agree a deal to lift the borrowing limit did little to boost prices 
however, which lurched sharply lower after a rating agency overlooked the deal and cut their assessment of US debt 
from its prior top notch.  At around the same time, fears that the European debt crisis would spread to Italy and Spain, in 
addition to France, all considered too big to fail, but significantly, too big to save, fanned fears that problems on both 
sides of the Atlantic would lead to a much talked about double-dip recession and consequently, weaker demand for 
industrial metals.  Meanwhile, the final pillar of support for current supply constraints was removed as workers at Chile’s 
Escondida agreed to go back to work after a two week stoppage, which left sentiment heavily weighed to the downside. 
Prices range bound in second half of month  Prices rallied strongly on 11th August, bouncing back after touching the 
lowest level this year the prior day, with the focus moving to Chinese trade and currency news.  Initial Chinese trade data 
pointed to a further recovery in imports of copper, which was confirmed later in the month, while at the same time the 
People’s Bank of China fixed its exchange rate against the US dollar at a new record, which combined to lift the markets’ 
mood.  With the arbitrage window open for most of the month, in addition to the stronger domestic currency, this is 
supportive of our view of recovering Chinese imports through the remainder of the year.  Following on from this 
aforementioned bounce on 11th, prices were largely directionless, ebbing between $8,700/t and $9,000/t through the 
remainder of the month. 
Threat of strike action looms large in the background  As we noted above, Escondida’s fortnight-long strike has 
ended but the threat of further disruptions elsewhere does loom large in the background, with workers at Collahuasi in 
Chile and at Freeport’s Grasberg mine in Indonesia poised to down tools.  The threat of a one day strike at Collahuasi on 
2nd September relates to workers wanting colleagues who were fired after a previous disruption re-hired, while Freeport 
Indonesia’s copper operations at Grasberg remain under threat of renewed strike action.  This follows the failure of talks 
between the company and union representatives to reach an agreement to establish a new contract covering 2012-2013 
once the one currently in force expires in October.  The two sides are reportedly far apart on even the basic elements to 
typical contract talks, and the possibility of a sudden halt to operations looms large, although there has been no 
indication of when such action will begin.

Stocks little changed through August  Exchange stock levels were little changed through the month overall, although 
Shanghai did edge slightly lower.  The London Metal Exchange ended last month with inventories standing at 466,025 
tonnes and remain at similar levels at the time or writing, with a pattern emerging of stocks edging slightly lower most 
days before a large shipment would break the declining streak.  Stocks would then tick modestly lower again before a 
further large intake.  On a regional basis, warehouses in Europe increased inventories but those in Asia and the US 
edged lower.  It was a similar story for Comex stocks, which ended the month broadly where they began. 
In Shanghai, SHFE stocks finished the month down just under 15kt, to close August on 102.258kt, reversing at least part 
of the increase from last month, while bonded warehouse stock levels also declined by around 50kt through the month 
and now stand at around 300kt.  Bonded warehouse stocks had increased by around 50kt the prior month, with part of 
the increase related to rising imports into China.

July, imports have maintained their recent improving streak to rise by 8.8% month on month in July to 194.3kt.  The rise 
followed favourable arbitrage conditions in April and May and despite the window closing in the subsequent two months, 
the situation changed yet again in August to make imports of LME material profitable again.  This fits neatly with our view 
of continued increases in imports of copper into China in the second half of the year.

Copper Monthly Update 
Chinese premia turn higher from month end slip  After slipping at the very end of the month, premia in China 
recovered to the $90-120/t range and point to firm demand conditions despite the usual seasonal slowdown.  Indeed, 
that the front month SHFE contract moved into backwardation relative to three month copper confirmed this view.  With 
the collapse in copper prices through August, scrap dealers became increasingly reluctant to sell material, resulting in 
scrap spreads tightening and direct use of scrap by semis producers declining.  As such, semis plants increased 
consumption of refined material, with this going some way to explaining the relative tightness in the market that firm 
premia suggest. 
European and US premia unmoved  In Europe and the US, premia barely changed this month, although little trade was 
conducted in any case with semis producers and traders in the middle of their summer holidays.  The movement of 
premia in the coming month will be interesting to watch as this will be the first indication of semis producer sentiment 
after the latest bout of panic associated with the European debt crisis.  There have been plenty of reports of downstream 
mills being cautious over the outlook and placing orders for only what they need and suggesting a further round of 
destocking.  However, with copper prices still at relatively high levels, there was little incentive for fabricators to keep 
anything other than what they need in any case and ordering on a hand to mouth basis is, therefore, business as usual.   
2011 global demand downgraded despite increase in China  We have made a number of changes to our demand 
forecasts since last month, with the net result that we now forecast global growth of 5.1% this year, compared to our 
previous forecast of 5.4%.  Although this change in itself is relatively modest, there have been more significant changes 
within this global number.  Of particular note, we have upgraded our estimate of Chinese demand to 9.2% from 5% 
previously, after detailed analyses of unreported stock changes.  Meanwhile, we have downgraded both Western 
European and US demand prospects for this year, to growth of 0.3% and 3% respectively.   
Lower starting point cuts Q4 price forecast  The lower estimate for 2011 consumption is, therefore, largely 
responsible for the change to our metal market balance, which now stands at a deficit of 351kt this year, compared to 
408kt in July.  Crucially, we still expect a deficit and the modest adjustment does not alter our view of fundamentally 
supported prices in the final part of the year.  What has changed, however, is the starting point.  At the time of writing 
prices hover just above $9,000/t after the collapse in the early part of August, and as a consequence we have a much 
lower starting point for prices to move from than was the case at the end of July when we wrote our last report.  As such, 
while we still expect prices to increase in the final quarter, we have lowered our forecast to $9,700/t from $10,000/t 
previously, in addition to cutting our estimate of Q3 prices to $9,200/t.  Our estimate of full year prices has also been 
reduced to $9,420/t, although we have maintained our forecast for 2012 at $9,588/t, with prices expected to peak in the 
second quarter in line with seasonal demand strength.  Prices will continue to be driven by economic news and related 
sentiment in the short term, while the direction of physical premia will likely be the first indicator of whether there has 
been any real impact to demand from the knock to confidence that the latest round of debt problems has caused.

Copper Monthly Update 
Consumption 
We have made a number of changes to our demand forecasts since last month, with the net result that we now forecast 
global demand growth of 5.1% this year, compared to our previous forecast of 5.4%.  Although this change in itself is 
relatively modest, there have been more significant changes within this global number.  Of particular note, we have 
upgraded our estimate of Chinese demand to 9.2% from 5% previously following detailed analysis of unreported stock 
changes.  Meanwhile, we have downgraded both Western European and US demand prospects for this year, to 0.3% 
and 3% respectively.   
Europe and CIS 
Western European demand outlook downgraded  Although we do not have a full set of first half data, we have a 
pretty good feel for activity in the January to June period of 2011 and this has led us to downgrade demand across much 
of the region.  Key changes include German growth being toned down from 4.9% to 3.6% this year, while for France and 
Spain our previous forecasts of positive growth this year have turned into expectations of full year contraction.  Overall, 
these changes result in Western European demand being little more than flat this year, with consumption in 2012 
improving in the region of 1%. 
Industrial slowdown begins to pinch in June  Although these downgrades come against the backdrop of the ongoing 
European debt crisis, they are not directly related to it.  We have always been of the view that industrial and economic 
activity will slow in the second half of the year but this perhaps came a little earlier than we anticipated.  Indeed, 
eurozone industrial production fell by 0.7% month on month in June, well short of analyst expectations of an increase of 
0.1%.  The decline was due to a 2.5% drop in durable consumer goods, while capital goods and intermediate goods also 
suffered, slipping 1.5% and 0.6%, respectively.  Output declined in both France and Germany. Year over year, eurozone 
industrial production rose by 2.9%, however.  The data showed that for the full 27 EU states there was an even greater 
decline of 1.2% month on month, with year-on-year growth of just 1.7%. 
Lead indicators point to further weakness Lead indicators suggest that further monthly falls in IP should be expected 
through the third quarter as weakness in consumer demand persists.  The preliminary eurozone PMI for August fell to 
49.7 from 50.35, dipping below the 50 expansion threshold for the first time since September 2009, while the new orders 
index hit a 2-year low of 46.9.   
Aurubis wire rod production slows in calendar Q2  The latest quarterly earnings results from cathode and semis 
producer Aurubis has revealed a decline in wire rod output of 5.7% year on year to 198kt in the second calendar quarter 
of the year.  This was also lower than first quarter output of 217kt.  However, softening the blow somewhat, production of 
copper shapes recovered from the first quarter dip to post a 10% year-on-year rise to 55kt.

midst of work and maintenance shutdowns.  More visibility into whether there has been any real impact from the ongoing

Copper Monthly Update 
Russian authorities introduce variable export duty  A variable duty has been introduced on exports of copper 
cathode from Russia, with the duty set to increase as the copper price rises.  Nothing will be payable on exports when 
the copper price is below $6,000/t, while a 10% duty will be applied when the price is in the range $6,000-$8,000/t.  At 
prices above $8,000/t, $800 plus 30% of the price above $8,000 will be payable.  This replaces the current rule where a 
10% tax is levied on all cathode exports, which was reintroduced this year and has indirectly resulted in a sharp rise in 
Russian apparent consumption of copper.  In a bid to avoid the export duty, firms are producing wire rod, thus increasing 
consumption, and exporting this instead of cathode.  Russian exports of refined copper were down by 68% in the first 
half of the year at 75.167kt, while wire rod exports more than doubled to 178.435kt in the same period.  We currently 
estimate apparent refined consumption growth of 57.4% to 700kt in 2011, although it must be noted that this simply puts 
Russian demand back on a par with 2008, the year before the previous cathode export tax was suspended. 
Americas 
Mixed bag of macrodata not enough to outweigh usual summer decline in US  The seasonal slowdown across the 
northern hemisphere was pretty evident in the USA, with select data highlighting factory closures and holiday periods.  
Total vehicle production fell sharply in July from the previous month, but on a seasonally-adjusted annualised rate output 
was up by 10% m-o-m to 8.73 million units, just shy of the level reached in March before operations were disrupted by 
parts shortages.  Total vehicle sales increased by 6% m-o-m in July (on a seasonally-adjusted basis) to 12.2M units, but 
this rate of sales is below the level of late 2010 and early 2011.  The improvement over May and June suggests that 
easing fuel prices are tempting consumers back into the market, even for the bigger-ticket items such as large SUVs. 
US unemployment remains stubbornly high, and is likely to do so with government job losses reducing the impact of 
private-sector creation last month.  Despite consumer confidence levels picking up a notch in July to 59.5, we would 
typically look for a reading of 90 to reflect a healthy state to the economy, so there is some way to go yet before we can 
satisfy this condition.  On a better note, however, US durable goods orders rose by 4% in July vs. the disappointing 2.1% 
contraction in June.  July’s rate benefited from high transportation equipment orders, with commercial aircraft doing 
particularly well.    
In the US housing market, starts fell by 1.5% m-o-m in July to an annual rate of 604,000, but were still up by 9.8% y-o-y. 
Building permits, which measure future building activity, fell by 3.2% m-o-m. It appears that housing starts are still 
struggling to gain momentum, especially with a decline in building permits.  Indeed, it is hard to imagine much of an 
improvement before the end of 2012.  To illustrate how far housing starts have to go, a healthy market would see these 
grow at an annual rate of approximately 1.2 million.  Meanwhile, existing-home sales fell 3.5% m-o-m in July to an annual 
rate of 4.67 million, an eight-month low.  Lawrence Yun, the National Association of Realtors’ chief economist, stated that 
although home prices are very favorable, buyers “…are being held back because banks are only offering financing to the 
most highly qualified borrowers.”   
Rod markets reflect summer slowdown  At the metals level, rod production levels for July of 96.7kt confirm the 
downtrend that has been in place since May, according to data from the American Bureau of Metals Statistics.  Equally, 
ABMS data also show the commensurate decline in rod shipments, from 108kt to 95kt in July.  Shipments for the first 
seven months of this year were down by 2.1% compared to the same period for 2010, to 744kt.  Meanwhile, revised data 
from the Copper and Brass Servicecenter Association show that distributors’ shipments to June have also stalled.  
During this first half, the CBSA’s members shipped an average of 10.2kt/m, no better than H1 2010.  The one upside is 
that some players believe that poor sales to the depressed construction sector are finally hitting bottom and stabilising, 
rather than showing potential for worsening.  Even so, we have taken the precaution of reducing our forecast copper 
demand for the USA this year slightly, to 1.813Mt from 1.841Mt, due to the weaker rod environment. 
Russian rod makes appearance in US market  For the first time since March 2009, the USA became a net importer of 
copper rod in June, thanks largely to an unexpected influx of rod from Russia.  We had previously reported that Russian 
cathode exports would shrink owing to the new export tax on the product from last December, and through to May most 
of the rod – having been converted from cathode by domestic producers to avoid the duty – had shown up in Europe, 
mainly in Turkey.  But if US rod markets were looking flat since May, no one told the Russians about it, and in May the 
first batch of imports from Russia (c.400t) since January 2009 showed up into the US ports of New Orleans and 
Baltimore.  This ballooned into 6.7kt in June, and is likely to stem US optimism for better rod prices as we head into the 
Q3 ordering period.  In the past, Russian material has come into the US market rather sporadically, but the additional 
export tax on cathode issued this month is likely to maintain cathode-to-rod conversion at home for some time, and 
hence higher than normal rod exports from Russia might well become more established for the rest of this year. 
Besides this Russian material, the formerly bankrupt Sherburne Metals copper rod mill in upstate NY should be re-
commissioned during October with the assistance of UpCast staff, and is likely to be active selling its own rod into the 
market by late-Q4.  This re-activation should add c.30kt capacity; the second line (15kt/a) is unlikely to receive attention 
from UpCast technical personnel as it was not an official UpCast line.

China 
Inflation prospects recede despite recent jump in prices  The recent trend of accelerating price inflation yet slowing 
industrial activity has continued into the latest available Chinese data set for July.  Consumer prices increased slightly in 
July and rocketing food prices are an ongoing source of discontent.  However, we do think that inflation is peaking in 
China and should begin to slow in the fourth quarter.  Meanwhile, industrial production rose by 14.0% year on year in 
July, slower than the 15.1% growth recorded in June but on par with growth through the first half.  Heavy industry rose by 
14.5%, while light industry expanded by 12.8%.  IP growth was 0.9% in month-on-month terms.  In contrast to 2008, the 
global slowdown is coming at a time when China is steaming ahead, and although Chinese export growth may slow it still 
does not seem likely that IP will be severely impacted.  
Chinese growth prospects upgraded  A detailed review of first half data has led to an upgrade in our estimate of full 
year growth in China this year.  Looking at apparent consumption statistics alone, without consideration of unreported 
stock movements, these fail to take into account the significant stock changes that typically take place in China through 
the year.  Indeed, it is a much shallower stock build in China in the first quarter this year than took place in 2010 that has 
resulted in real demand rising by 7.3% in Q1 by our estimates.  When stripping out stock movements this would have 
been a contraction of around 6% in the same period.  This was also a feature of second quarter demand data, with real 
demand estimated to have grown by some 13.8%, compared to a simple apparent consumption calculation which 
reveals an 8% contraction.  For the full year we now expect growth in refined copper consumption of 9.2% in 2011, 
slowing to 7% the following year. 
Imports continue steady uptick  It is difficult to characterise the improvement of imports into China as anything other 
than steady; however, this still offers comfort to our full year forecast.  If anything, imports into China this year have been 
the major disappointment, although since May they have at least been improving.  Latest data for July revealed imports 
were still lower by some 14.5% on a year-on-year basis at 190.5kt but on an upward monthly trend, boosted by the 
SHFE/LME arbitrage window opening up in the preceding months.  After closing again over the last couple of months, 
the window has reopened as of late, pointing to continued improvement in the months to come.  That one of the 
measures China is using to fight inflation is to allow its currency to appreciate only favours our assessment of further 
gains in imports as foreign material becomes relatively less expensive.  The favourable arbitrage, in addition to sharp 
declines seen over the past month, have led to semis producers stocking up on cathode in August.  As a result, bonded 
warehouse stocks ebbed lower again in August by around 50kt and now stand at around 300kt after edging higher by a 
similar amount in the previous month.   
Build up of wire rod stocks  Heading into August anecdotal evidence suggested that there was a build up of stocks of 
wire rod at mills and that despite this, firms have been maintaining output at relatively high levels.  There is no obvious 
reason why a company would continue to produce significantly ahead of order levels except in the very short term as 
amassing stocks of finished goods would simply increase working capital requirements and with copper prices so high, 
this does not make a lot of sense.  However, there may also be a difference between the state owned enterprises and 
the private sector in China in the sense that the SOE rod plants will be funded by local banks and will simply “spend” 
their budget allocations in terms of buying cathodes and produce whatever they can regardless of whether or not there is 
an immediate market for this wire rod.

It is also worth mentioning that the massive end-use growth rates seen in China over the past few years has meant that 
pipeline stocks of all intermediaries must have been substantial over an extended period of time.  Clearly, if end-use 
demand growth has tapered off then stocks of wire rod will certainly appear to be high relative to off-take.  Meanwhile, 
perhaps some firms were producing at high rates in anticipation of summer power outages, which led to a stock build.  In 
all likelihood, the real explanation is a combination of all of the above. 
Affordable homes target cut for 2012  China has reportedly cut its target for the construction of affordable homes to be

Industrial activity continues on recovery track  The Japanese industrial sector appears to be recovering at a faster 
pace than initially expected, with latest data for industrial output underscoring this point.  In fact, IP rose by 3.8% month

Japanese demand upgraded following stronger than expected Q2  In the wake of the disasters that struck Japan in 
March we had lowered our estimate of consumption in Japan for the full year.  However, to our surprise, semis output 
maintained a firm pace through the April to June period as the construction of temporary homes boosted shipments, 
despite weakness in the transport and electronics sectors.  As a result, we have upgraded our view of apparent demand 
for the full year in Japan to a contraction of 2%, compared to our previous estimate of decline of some 6%.

slipping on the prior month.  On a sectoral basis, construction disappointed, posting its first year-on-year fall in a year, 
while autos also registered a further fall on the year ago figure, however, the volume was the highest level since 
February.  For the year to July, shipments were just negative, although on a brighter note, production of wire and cable 
has fared better this year.  Indeed, production was up by 3.9% in the first half of the year, buoyed by stronger output of 
power cable. 
Japanese vehicle output continues to recover…  June auto production decreased by 14% year on year, a vast 
improvement over the average decline of 50% in the preceding 3 months.  Toyota recently commented that restoration 
has occurred at a faster-than-expected speed.  It plans to hire up to 4000 contract workers in Japan to help make up for 
lost ground and output should have fully recovered by September.  Toyota estimates the quake will reduce annual output 
by 150,000 units, down by 2/3rds from its previous estimates.

China’s 7M 2011 concentrate imports down by 10.7% on a year earlier  According to official customs statistics, 
Chinese copper concentrate imports were 452.6kdmt in July, which represents a decline of 3.7% on the same month last 
year.  Moreover, on a cumulative basis through the first seven months of 2011, the country’s overall receipts remained 
suppressed relative to last year, being lower by 10.7% at 3.4Mdmt.  Chile’s contribution remained significantly less  
(-29.7%) than in 2010 due to lower output at Escondida, port problems at Collahuasi etc.  Turkey also recorded a 
sizeable reduction in shipments (-61.1%) in part due to the reactivation of the 30kt/a Samsun facility.  The owners of this 
plant have also installed a dedicated copper refinery (previously the smelter’s blister output was sold to traders).   
Ramp up of new Chinese smelting capacity should result in higher concentrate imports  Earlier we mentioned 
declining concentrate stockpiles in China as being a contributor to falling spot TC/RCs.  There are a number of reasons 
for this.  Firstly, the 200kt/a Kunming smelter belonging to Yunnan Copper was re-started in February 2010 after having 
been out of operation for 231 days (41 days less than anticipated).  The official reason for the closure was to fully 
overhaul the IsaSmelt furnace and ancillary equipment; however, some market commentators believed that another 
reason for the long shutdown was due to depressed TC/RCs.  Elsewhere, Daye commissioned its new Ausmelt furnace, 
which has a greater capacity than the previous configuration.  More recently, in Q2 2011 the capacity of the Xiangguang 
smelter in Shandong province was doubled from 200kt/a to 400kt/a.  Elsewhere, a number of projects have been 
ramping up production this year, including the 100kt/a Tianzhong plant in Yunnan, which has replaced an old 35kt/a blast 
furnace operation, Hengbang in Sichuan province (50kt/a), Houma in Shanxi province (+50kt/a), Kunpeng in Sichuan 
province (100kt/a) and Yunnan Tin in Yunnan province (100kt/a).  Finally, Zijin Mining’s 200kt/a smelter in Fujian 
province is expected to be commissioned during the latter stages of Q4.  
Chinese raw materials stocks built up in 2010 have now halved  Below is an update of an analysis of raw material 
stock movements based upon official CNIA data.  This shows the make-up of refined production from primary and 
secondary sources.  We have removed imported blister from the CNIA secondary production data as this appears to be 
included in these statistics.  We have then compared the primary refined production figures with the various components 
that make up this number, i.e. from domestic and imported concentrates, SxEw and imported blister and matte.  Note 
that these figures are shown on a recoverable basis (i.e. net of 3.4% overall smelting losses where appropriate).  This 
comparison allows us to calculate an implied stock change for each year.  What this shows is that there has been an

Forecast refined output dropped by 65kt  Since our last report we have dropped our forecast 2011 refined copper 
production capability by 65kt, with the main reductions coming in Latin America (-56kt) and Asia (-33kt) being only

of whom were prior direct employees of the state-owned entity).  However, looking towards the rest of this year and 
probably into 2012, this particular issue may not be as prominent given the late-August agreement between contracting 
companies and their employees, which ensures bonus payments, presumably if certain conditions are met.   
Overall, Chilean copper output for H1 was down by 2.2%, to 2.571Mt as heavy rains and technical issues at various 
mines and associated mills took almost 150kt copper out of Q1 targets this year.  Xstrata Copper’s Collahuasi was one of 
the mines most affected by the inclement weather as well as previously reported port issues, as output fell by 12.1% 
during H1 2011 year on year to 234.5kt from 266.7kt.  Equally, Teck’s Quebrada Blanca also suffered from the rains, and 
produced 27% less copper during H1 (32.1kt vs 44kt during the same period 2010).  Output at BHPB’s Minera 
Escondida, meanwhile, fell by over 14% to 450.7kt from 526kt, primarily due to technical problems affecting a conveyor 
belt and SAG mill during the first quarter.  On the other hand, better performances came from Candelaria (up by almost 
33% during H1 to 71kt) and from the small mines sector (up by 31.5%, to 220.2kt).

operations at Grasberg remain under threat of renewed strike action as we end this month, following the failure of talks

balances that catches the eye of the market and follows through to prices.  However, with the mine going through a 
transitional phase regarding its ore profile, the daily impact will be somewhat less this year and into 2012 than prior 
years, when output has ranged between 600-800kt.  Even so, from reported details it appears that the two sides remain 
far apart on even the basic elements to typical contract talks, and the possibility of a sudden halt to operations looms

Aurubis Pirdop cathode output catches up in fiscal Q3  Aurubis’ Primary Copper Business Unit produced a recent 
record amount of cathode during the company’s fiscal Q3 (Apr-Jun), at 238kt, narrowly beating the prior quarter’s 233kt 
and maintaining what have been remarkably consistent quarterly production performances across the three principal 
sites which comprise the Primary Copper Unit.  For the nine months to June, the Unit produced 696kt cathode (down 1% 
on the comparable period), with 22% higher scrap use offsetting 2% lower concentrate throughput; meanwhile, cathode 
output from the Recycling Business Unit remained the same at 160kt, with the new KRS-Plus system at Luenen being 
available for part of the recent period and allowing material processed to increase by 9%.   
The Bulgarian site in Pirdop has recovered well since the planned smelter outage of the first fiscal quarter (Oct-Dec 
2010).  Then, Pirdop produced 50kt of cathodes, but this increased to 57kt in fiscal Q3, bringing the nine-month period 
up to 164kt and matching the amount produced in the comparable 2009-2010 period.  The plant remains on track to 
reach a record output level of 225kt or so this calendar year, beating 2010’s prior record of 216kt and extending the year-
on-year gains that have been witnessed since 2000.  Meanwhile, the impact of the unscheduled stoppage last December 
at the Hamburg site also looks like it will largely be overcome within this calendar year.  Hamburg produced 269kt of 
cathodes from the tankhouse, down from 281kt in the prior year.  However, some work that was to be carried out during 
the statutory overhaul of autumn 2011 was carried out when the smelter was out of action last December.  Consequently, 
we anticipate a return to the past averages of 375-380kt this year for Hamburg, rather than the 355kt of 2010.  In its 
2009/10 annual report the company referred to an expansion at its Hamburg smelter and tankhouse and for the 2012 
calendar year, we anticipate Hamburg will be able to reach a new record refined output in excess of 410kt.  This is in part 
due to the commissioning of the KRS-Plus furnace at Luenen this year, which should mean that fewer anodes will be 
sent from Hamburg to Luenen, leaving c.40kt/a more anodes available for conversion locally. 
Norilsk poor Q2 keeps the company on a declining track  Refined copper output for the first half of this year of only 
176.5kt combined for its Monchegorsk and Norilsk units vs. 185.3kt for H1 2010 is keeping the company on a declining 
track for the sixth consecutive year.  This is largely a reflection of mining less copper-rich ore at Norilsk’s Komsomolsky 
and Oktyabrysky mines over recent years, resulting in refined metal output there falling from 361kt in 2005 to just 309kt 
last year (although the 2005 result also included production from what had been a large stockpile of concentrates).  2011 
will see little change, with our expectation being slightly below 300kt, but the company is planning to install new 
equipment during this second half to allow for an increase in copper-rich ore processing from next year.  This should lift 
the unit’s refined copper output back to 2010 levels of 305-310kt for the 2012-2013 period, before a more sustainable 
rise to 315-325kt is reached through to 2015.  Refined output at Monchegorsk, however, relies on matte from Pechenga 
and from Norilsk and is expected to remain flat in the 60kt/a region (58kt anticipated this year) for the next decade.

Inmet reduces expectations for Las Cruces  In what has emerged to be a difficult quarter for Toronto-based Inmet 
Mining, the company has downgraded its expectations of full-year 2011 copper cathode output from its Las Cruces 
property in Spain.  Following the 16-day scheduled start-up, which initially gave promising results, a support structure at 
the new grinding thickener failed due to a faulty weld, causing another seven-day outage for repairs.  The company’s 
new guidance for the plant now stands at between 42-45kt for this year, down from 50kt.  On a brighter note, the 
company’s board approved a development decision at Cobre Panama, subject to certain milestones being achieved, and 
Inmet has already engaged various companies with regards to becoming new partners in the project, which could 
become a potential 300kt/a producer by 2016. 
Teck looks to improve at Andacollo  Despite the increase in copper in concentrate production since its commercial 
start-up last October, Teck Resources remains disappointed with aspects of the new mill at Carmen de Andacollo in 
Chile, and will spend a further US$15m on improvements.  During Q2, throughput at the concentrator was c.39kt/d in 
comparison with a design capacity of 55kt/d.  Teck will install a small crusher to feed coarse ore to the pebble crusher by 
the end of this month.  In Q3, the SAG mill motor capacity will be uprated by 10%, and during Q1 next year a 20kt/d pre-
crusher plant will be installed, all steps intended to exploit the design capacity of the mill itself.  By the end of this year, 
the company should also complete studies looking into adding a second SAG mill, ball mill and associated equipment in 
order to increase Andacollo’s potential output to between 100-120kt/a from the currently anticipated 80kt/a.  Output of 
copper in concentrates for H1 2011 reached 33kt, but little ramp-up improvement has been noted at the mine and it is 
likely to produce only c.65kt this year.  2011 will also be the last year that Andacollo produces copper in cathode form 
due to ore type transition: just 7kt are expected this year (1.4kt in Q2), after 14 years of producing an average 20kt/a in 
cathode. 
Kazakhmys confirms development of Boschekul  This month Kazakhmys PLC confirmed it will press ahead with the 
development of the Boschekul (Bozshakol) copper deposit in northern Kazakhstan at a capex of US$1.8Bn.  There will 
be a three-year development phase at the mine, beginning later this year.  Pre-production will start in 2014, with initial 
ores being treated at the associated concentrator the following year.  This is slightly ahead of prior announcements, as 
we were not expecting any material output of concentrates to become available until early 2016.  Located 250km east of 
the capital Astana, Boschekul will be an open pit with a potential mine life of 39 years.  It has a mineral resource of 
1.173Bnt assaying 0.35% Cu, and is expected to provide between 90-100kt/a copper in concentrates over the first 14 
years of operation from the Central Pit, dropping to averages closer to 80kt/a from then on.  Elsewhere, Kazakhmys has 
also begun a feasibility study on the Aktogay resource and expects to make a further decision on this once the results 
are available by mid-2012.  This could also become a significant 100kt/a copper in concentrate producer by 2017. 
Glencore’s Cobar suffers in Q2 – grants new contract to MacMahon…  Glencore’s 100%-owned subsidiary, Cobar 
Management Pty Ltd, issued a A$110M contract to West Australia-based engineering company MacMahon for services 
at its CSA mine in New South Wales.  Over the next two years, MacMahon will oversee all design engineering, 
fabrication, procurement construction and management of the extension and upgrade of the CSA No.1 shaft.  This will 
take the existing shaft down from the 1015m level to 1550m, and will also incorporate a new headframe with tower-
mounted friction winder and the construction of a new underground materials handling system, including crusher, ore 
bins, conveyors and loading system.  This should allow CSA to see the back of the current issues at the mine, which 
reduced H1 output to 21kt copper in concentrates from 26kt for the equivalent period of a year ago.  Forecast output for 
this year is 10% down on prior forecasts of c.53kt to 48kt, but the MacMahon contract should allow CSA to access more 
ore and increase production by 2013. 
..turns out rapid ramp-up at Mutanda…  In the Democratic Republic of Congo, Glencore’s 40%-held subsidiary, 
Mutanda Mining, has managed to reach its initial nameplate capacity of 20kt cathode ahead of schedule, and has even 
proceeded with the commissioning of Phase II, which will see an additional 40kt/a coming available via electrowinning 
tankhouses 2 and 3.  Copper mining has also been increased to match the higher available processing capacity, allowing 
total copper production to reach 25.8kt during this first half in both cathode and metal in concentrate forms.  A revised 
full-year estimate of 62kt has now been forecast for Mutanda (with 42kt of this coming in cathode form), which is 
significantly above the prior overall guideline of 42kt.  Mutanda should be producing c.110kt/a cathode (and 23kt cobalt in 
hydroxide) by Q2 2012, as the addition of EW 4 comes into operation by the end of this year. 
..and adds on SX plant at Luilu earlier than planned  During the second quarter, Glencore’s near 75%-owned 
subsidiary, Katanga Mining, completed engineering studies for a phase 4 expansion at Katanga.  The group has 
concluded that an additional 100kt/a SX plant should be built at Luilu, taking total copper output at Katanga to 310kt/a.  It 
will also require the construction of an in-pit crusher at KOV Open Pit.  These two extras will add a further US$93M to the 
former capex identified for Phase 4 expansion at Katanga, which now totals US$630M.
